beats.script_body: St. Mark's Place ends at Tompkins Square, the scene of the first labor demonstration in 1874 and a performance space for Jimi Hendrix and other 1960s legends. The square sat at the edge of an East Village that, a decade later, would help birth American punk — bands like the Ramones and Blondie playing the now-defunct CBGB nightclub on the Bowery, once one of the slummiest areas of the city.

beats.script_body: The Tredwells' 1832 Federal-style row house is reportedly Manhattan's most haunted house. Each month from January to October it presents Candlelight Ghost Tours, in which Gertrude Tredwell — the last family owner, who died in 1933 — is summoned from the great beyond. By day, eight rooms over three floors keep the family's fixtures, furnishings, decorative arts, and personal possessions exactly as they left them, the city's only 19th-century home to retain its original interior and exterior.

beats.script_body: Union Square lies at the intersection — the union — of Broadway and Fourth Avenue, marking Greenwich Village's northeastern tip. Its 6.5-acre park hosts a popular farmers' market on Mondays, Wednesdays, Fridays, and Saturdays, where you can sample local bread, cheese, wine, and crafts; in November and December the Union Square Holiday Market takes over with jewelry, candles, ornaments, and Christmas décor.

beats.script_body: Once the home of the meat trade, this cluster of streets is now Manhattan's trendiest quarter, a backdrop to some of the city's coolest restaurants, most exclusive clubs, and most expensive shops — though you might still spot a few surviving meatpacking houses among the modern glass architecture. Along 14th Street you can window-shop the high-end boutiques of Diane von Furstenberg, Jeffrey New York, and Christian Louboutin, while just to the north lie the 35-plus upscale food vendors of Chelsea Market.

beats.script_body: This slimline park sits 30 feet above the ground, created along 1.45 miles of disused freight track. Miniature landscapes — wildflower meadows among them — line the walking trail from Gansevoort Street to West 34th Street; en route you can pause on wooden loungers and viewing platforms and take in temporary art installations. With views of the Hudson River and the streets below, the High Line is a special place to watch the sun set over the city.

beats.script_body: New York's literary roots trace to Washington Irving, considered the first American to make a living from writing. Famous for the short story "Rip Van Winkle," Irving was born and raised in post-colonial Manhattan. In 1807 he launched the satirical literary magazine Salmagundi, in which he coined the term "Gotham" as a pseudonym for New York — a nickname that has clung to the city ever since.

beats.script_body: By the 1950s, New York was abuzz with literary talent, including poet Allen Ginsberg and novelists Jack Kerouac and Norman Mailer. Truman Capote published Breakfast at Tiffany's in 1958, and James Baldwin published Another Country — set in Harlem and Greenwich Village — in 1962. In recent decades, figures such as the Bronx-born Don DeLillo and Brooklyn resident Paul Auster have dominated the city's literary scene.

beats.script_body: Known to locals simply as "the Village," the world-famous neighborhood originally really was a village. By the late 19th century, literary salons, art clubs, and cutting-edge theaters were flourishing here, a radical, bohemian spirit that has drawn some of the most creative minds in politics and the arts since the early 19th century.

By the late 19th century, literary salons, art clubs, and cutting-edge theaters were flourishing... The neighborhood's radical, bohemian spirit has attracted some of the most creative minds in politics and the arts since the early 19th century.

beats.script_body: Once an immigrant neighborhood, the East Village acquired its distinctive feel in the 1960s as the haunt of artists, musicians, and hippies, and as the center of America's counterculture. It was home to writers of the Beat Generation in the 1950s; with the rise of 1960s counterculture, hippies moved in where immigrants had once settled. Gentrification has since erased some of the area's grittiness, but its artsy vibe survives in graffiti-covered walls and independent stores.

review_queue.description: Union Square George Washington equestrian statue: book says 'Cast in 1814'; auto-corrected to 1856 in the beat body (2+ independent sources: Wikipedia, NYC Parks). The 'oldest sculpture in NYC parks collection' claim is correct and retained.
review_queue.recommendation: Accept the 1856 correction (already applied; logged in beat corrections).

review_queue.description: Washington Square Arch Duchamp stunt: book attributes the 1917 arch climb to the 'Liberal Club' and states the arch is '86-foot-tall'. Sources name the group the 'Arch Conspirators' (Drick, Sloan, Duchamp + 3 actors) and give the arch height as ~73 ft 6 in. Core event (1917 Duchamp proclamation) is real; not auto-corrected because it touches attribution/measurement, not a deletable factual error with clean 2-source convergence on the exact phrasing.
review_queue.recommendation: Human review: keep the beat but consider editing 'Liberal Club' → 'a group of Village bohemians' and dropping the '86-foot' figure before upload.
